title: Cramér–Rao Bound
subtitle: How precise could an estimate possibly be?
body:
AN INTERACTIVE FIELD GUIDE

Precision has
a floor.

The Cramér–Rao Bound connects
what measurements reveal
to what estimators can achieve.

From repeated noisy measurements to Fisher information, bias, and the geometry of localization.
notes: Suggested pacing: 30–40 minutes including experiments. The main prerequisites are expectation, variance, derivatives, and basic matrices. Start by asking: “Could a cleverer algorithm always beat today’s error?” The answer depends on the measurement model and the estimator class. The scalar CRB is a pointwise frequentist lower bound, not a guarantee that an estimator attaining it exists. The browser deck is self-contained and works offline; the PDF and PowerPoint are static snapshots. Use arrow keys to navigate, O for overview, N for these notes, and F for fullscreen. Each lab preserves state while you navigate.

title: An estimate is one outcome. Precision is a distribution.
subtitle: Keep the unknown parameter fixed. Repeat the entire measurement process.
body:
01

A fixed world

The unknown value θ does not change between trials.

02

New measurements

Each trial produces a fresh random dataset X.

03

A new estimate

Apply the same rule T(X). Its spread is the variance.

The estimator

Unbiased means correct on average, across repeated datasets.

The question

How narrow can that cloud be?

Not “How close was this single estimate?”
Not “How small is the observation noise?”
notes: Make the distinction between a measurement distribution and a sampling distribution explicit. A sample of 16 observations is one trial, not 16 estimates. Monte Carlo repeats the entire trial many times. The CRB constrains the estimator variance at a fixed true parameter when unbiasedness holds in a neighborhood and regularity conditions permit the score identity. It does not impose a minimum absolute error on each realized estimate.

title: Nearby worlds are hard to tell apart.
subtitle: Information measures how sensitively the data distribution changes when the parameter moves.
body:
Same separation · different noise

Could these observations tell you which world is true?

These are data densities, not posterior probabilities.

From ambiguity to precision

Small changes must leave a detectable trace.

If θ and θ + δ generate almost indistinguishable data, a locally unbiased estimator cannot be arbitrarily concentrated.

Fisher information turns local sensitivity into a number. Larger information permits a lower variance bound.
notes: The word local matters. Fisher information describes infinitesimal changes in the distribution around the true parameter; it can miss distant competing likelihood modes. The two curve pairs use the same mean displacement and different known Gaussian noise levels. This is an intuition illustration, not a classifier or a posterior. In the Gaussian location model the information per observation is exactly 1/σ². That calculation will appear shortly.

title: Likelihood → score → Fisher information.
subtitle: The likelihood is a function of the candidate parameter, with the observed dataset held fixed.
body:
1 · Likelihood

How compatible is a candidate?

A likelihood is not automatically a probability distribution over θ.

2 · Score

Which way does the evidence push?

Under regularity, Eθ[Uθ] = 0.

3 · Fisher information

Expected squared score = expected curvature

The curvature identity requires additional differentiability and interchange conditions.
notes: I_n always means total information in the whole dataset. I_1 is reserved for one observation. The expected Fisher information is a model property evaluated at the true parameter. Observed information is minus the second derivative of the realized log likelihood and is generally random. They coincide in the known-variance Gaussian mean example, but not in every model. A normalized likelihood plotted with maximum 1 is not a posterior density.

title: The scalar Cramér–Rao Bound.
subtitle: A floor for the variance of locally unbiased estimators in a regular model.
body:
The bound

Variance has squared parameter units.
Standard deviation has parameter units.

Read the fine print

The theorem has a scope.

Unbiasedness: Eθ[T] = θ in a neighborhood.

Regularity: differentiate under the expectation; the score has mean zero.

Finite information: 0 < Iₙ(θ) < ∞; T has finite variance.

Known model: the likelihood describes the actual experiment.
notes: An accessible sufficient setting is an interior parameter in a smooth family with parameter-independent support, dominated derivatives that justify differentiation under integration, finite positive Fisher information, and a finite-variance estimator. These are sufficient conditions rather than a complete necessary checklist. Local unbiasedness at θ means both the correct expectation and derivative equal to one there. A bound does not promise attainability. No single realized error or finite Monte Carlo variance is required to sit above the theoretical floor.

title: One score identity. One Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
subtitle: An unbiased estimator must move, on average, at the same rate as the true parameter.
body:
The score identity
1

2

3

Use Eθ[Uθ] = 0:

Cauchy–Schwarz

Correlation cannot exceed one.

The entire lower bound follows from how strongly an unbiased estimator must respond to the score.
notes: Because T is a statistic that does not itself depend on the unknown θ, differentiation acts on the density. Formally, ∂θ Eθ[T] = ∫ T(x) ∂θp(x;θ) dx = Eθ[TUθ]. Score mean zero follows by differentiating ∫ p(x;θ)dx = 1 under the integral. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives the result. For a biased statistic with expectation m(θ), replace 1 by m′(θ). That yields the biased extension used later. Regularity is not decorative: the uniform example breaks this step.

title: For a Gaussian mean, averaging is already optimal.
subtitle: Assume independent measurements Xi ∼ N(μ, σ²), with σ known.
body:
Compute the information
Compare with an estimator

The sample mean meets the bound exactly.

No asymptotic approximation is needed.
For this model, equality holds for every n ≥ 1.
notes: The Gaussian location family with known positive variance is regular. Each observation contributes information 1/σ². The sample mean has exact distribution N(μ,σ²/n), so it is unbiased and efficient at every sample size. This is not a generic statement about maximum likelihood estimators. The first-observation estimator X₁ is also unbiased, but discards n−1 measurements and has variance σ². Its efficiency relative to the full-data CRB is 1/n.

title: What will happen when you collect more measurements?
subtitle: In the next slide, every histogram bar comes from genuinely simulated datasets.
body:
Try these three moves

Predict → change → explain

16 → 64 samples: what happens to variance and standard deviation?

Double σ: which quantity gets four times larger?

Use only X₁: does collecting unused data improve that estimator?

Reference experiment

Independent Gaussian measurements

samples / trial

The truth is fixed across trials. Randomness comes only from new observations.
notes: Ask the audience to give both variance and standard-deviation answers. Quadrupling n divides variance by four and standard deviation by two. Doubling σ multiplies variance by four and standard deviation by two. Collecting more data does not help an estimator that ignores it. A finite empirical variance can fall slightly below the theoretical bound simply from Monte Carlo fluctuation. The live display distinguishes exact estimator variance, sample variance over trials, and the full-data bound.

title: Can you reach the precision floor?
subtitle: Change the experiment, repeat it, and compare empirical spread with the exact bound.
body:
Sampling distribution · one estimate per trial
Simulated estimatesEfficient mean referenceChosen estimator, exact
—across repeated trials
—theoretical, not fitted
—σ² / n, using all data

A simulated variance slightly below the CRB is Monte Carlo fluctuation, not a violation.

Independent N(μ, σ²) data

Truth μ = 1 stays fixed.
Parameter changes replay 2,000 trials from the chosen seed.
notes: Begin with the sample mean, n=16 and σ=2. The empirical variance should be near 0.25. Slide n to 64: the exact variance and CRB become 0.0625. Select “First observation”: its variance is now 4 even though the full-data CRB remains 0.0625. The teal curve is the exact efficient sample-mean density for this Gaussian model, not a universal probability distribution associated with a CRB. The rust dashed curve is the chosen estimator’s exact density. At the default estimator these two curves coincide. The code draws all n measurements independently using a seeded Box–Muller generator. Empirical variance uses divisor R−1; more trials reduce Monte Carlo variation. Reset restores defaults and exactly replays the initial 2,000 trials.

title: Four times the data. Half the standard deviation.
subtitle: Information adds for independent measurements; variance and standard deviation scale differently.
body:
Gaussian scaling · σ = 2
The useful arithmetic
nVariance boundSD bound

640.06250.25

The iid shortcut fails for correlated or non-identical data. Use the information of the joint likelihood.
notes: For independent but non-identical regular observations, information is the sum of their individual information contributions. The nI₁ formula additionally assumes identical information. Correlation does not automatically imply less information for every possible model, but it invalidates counting repeated correlated observations as independent. In a Gaussian mean model with known covariance R, information is 1ᵀR⁻¹1. The two plotted curves have different units and are separately labeled: variance in squared parameter units, SD in parameter units.

title: A narrow cloud can be centered in the wrong place.
subtitle: The unbiased CRB is not a universal lower bound on mean squared error.
body:
Bias–variance decomposition
The correct biased extension

The derivative of the bias matters.

This follows from the same proof, replacing 1 by ∂θEθ[T].
notes: Derivation: write m(θ)=Eθ[T]=θ+b(θ), so Cov(T,U)=m′(θ)=1+b′(θ). Cauchy–Schwarz gives the biased variance lower bound, and adding squared bias gives the MSE bound. This is a fixed-estimator, differentiable-bias statement; neither the estimator nor its tuning rule can secretly use the unknown true θ. A biased estimator can have MSE below the unbiased CRB at some θ, without contradiction. In the lab the shrinkage factor is selected by the viewer to inspect pointwise performance, not optimized by an estimator that knows μ.

title: Can you “beat” the bound by shrinking toward zero?
subtitle: Watch the variance fall, then move the true mean away from the shrinkage target.
body:
Exact sampling distributions · no Monte Carlo
Unbiased sample meanShrinkage estimatorTrue μ
—α²σ² / n
—(1 − α)²μ²
—variance + squared bias
Tα = α X̄ · target = 0

n = 16 and σ = 2, so the unbiased variance bound is 0.25.

Fixed α; no prior is assumed. A lower MSE here is a pointwise bias–variance tradeoff, not a violation of the unbiased CRB.
notes: The model has n=16, σ=2, so v=σ²/n=0.25. The shrinkage estimator is Tα=αX̄. It has expectation αμ, bias (α−1)μ, variance α²v, and MSE α²v+(1−α)²μ². Its bias derivative is α−1, so the biased variance bound is exactly α²v and is attained. At α=0 the distribution is a point mass at zero: the plot draws a spike, not a Gaussian density with zero variance. Try μ=0.35 then μ=2 with α=0.55; the same reduction in variance becomes a large bias penalty. The plots and metrics are analytic, not simulated. A prior is not needed for this example; the zero anchor is just a fixed shrinkage target.

title: “Lower bound” does not mean “always achievable.”
subtitle: Equality requires a very specific relationship between the estimator and the score.
body:
Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz

All estimation error aligns with the score.

For uniform attainment, this must define the same statistic T(X) throughout the parameter range.

Three distinct claims

Do not collapse them into one.

Unbiased: expectation equals the target.

Efficient: variance attains the CRB.

MLE: maximizes the likelihood; it may be biased at finite n.

Regular MLEs often approach the bound asymptotically. Finite-sample equality needs its own check.
notes: The displayed equality condition is for the scalar unbiased bound at the parameter value being considered, with nonzero finite information. Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz forces T−θ to be proportional to U; covariance 1 fixes the constant to 1/I. To attain the bound for every parameter, the right side plus θ must not require knowing the unknown θ. Asymptotic normality is a distributional statement; translating it into variance convergence requires appropriate moment control. Avoid claiming finite-sample MLE optimality merely from the asymptotic theorem.

title: Information has directions.
subtitle: A vector parameter has a covariance matrix—not a single uncertainty number.
body:
Matrix CRB

The vector score is u = ∇θ log p(X; θ).

The inequality holds in every direction q.
Assume J is nonsingular and the vector estimator is locally unbiased.

Eigenvectors tell the story

Large information eigenvalue → small variance bound along that eigenvector.
notes: Here u=∇θ log p(X;θ) is the score vector, and J is the total Fisher information matrix. The symbol ≽ denotes positive-semidefinite order: every quadratic form of Cov−J⁻¹ is nonnegative. It is not an element-by-element comparison. For positive-definite J, covariance-bound eigenvalues are reciprocal information eigenvalues. A covariance ellipse is a geometric visualization; probability coverage requires a distributional assumption and the appropriate radius. We use unit Mahalanobis radius and do not label it as a confidence region.

title: One range measurement constrains one local direction.
subtitle: A simplified 2D ranging model: known anchor positions, independent Gaussian range noise.
body:
The measurement model

Each rank-one term adds information along a line of sight. Here uᵢ is a unit direction, not the score vector.

Local sensitivity

A small radial move changes the range to first order. A tangential move does not.

The target must not coincide with an anchor. Noise variance is assumed known and independent of position.
notes: Differentiate h_i(p)=||p−a_i||. Its gradient is the unit vector from anchor i to the target. For independent additive Gaussian noise of known, position-independent variance, information is the sum of σ_i⁻² times the outer product of that gradient. This toy model starts from noisy ranges, not raw waveforms; it is inspired by localization-information geometry but is not a reproduction of the full wideband model in Shen and Win. With constant range-noise variance, moving an anchor along the same ray changes neither its information direction nor weight. Real range accuracy may depend on distance, SNR, multipath, or visibility.

title: Same sensors. Different geometry. Different limits.
subtitle: Four accurate ranges can still leave one position direction poorly constrained.
body:
Try these configurations

What should the uncertainty ellipse do?

Surround: place anchors in different directions.

Cluster: move them to almost the same line of sight.

Collinear: place anchors and target on one straight line.

Then turn on an unknown common range offset. How much position information is lost?

The scalar summary

Position error bound

For an unbiased position estimator:
root mean squared Euclidean error ≥ PEB.

A finite ellipse describes local information. It does not rule out distant mirror solutions.
notes: The PEB is the square root of trace J⁻¹ and has distance units. It lower-bounds RMSE of the full Euclidean position error, under the relevant unbiasedness and regularity conditions. It is neither a 95% radius nor the mean Euclidean error. Four anchors arranged in a line can still give full local rank when the target is off that line, even though a global reflection ambiguity remains. The preset named Collinear puts both anchors and target on the same line to deliberately produce local rank one. The demo reports singularity rather than drawing a falsely finite uncertainty ellipse.

title: Move the sensors. Reshape the bound.
subtitle: Drag any anchor or the target. The Fisher matrix and its inverse update immediately.
body:
Known anchors · local information at the true target
Anchors A1–A4True target PCRB ellipse

Unit-Mahalanobis CRB ellipse; not a confidence region.
notes: Drag or use the selection and coordinate sliders; every operation is accessible without pointer dragging. Coordinates and σ are in meters. The four anchor directions define J=Σuᵢuᵢᵀ/σ². The target is the true evaluation point, not a fitted estimate. With the common-offset toggle, the displayed matrix is the equivalent position information J_e after eliminating β by a Schur complement. The ellipse is centered at the truth and has principal radii 1/√λ; it is not simulated estimator output or a confidence ellipse. If eigenvalues are numerically zero, the UI gives a rank-deficient status and no finite PEB. Near-anchor coincidence is flagged because the range derivative fails there. Long ellipses can extend beyond the field of view; this is explicitly labeled. No nonlinear localization solver is being claimed.

title: An unknown clock offset consumes position information.
subtitle: The same measurements must now explain both the target position and a common range offset β.
body:
Partition the information

The position block of J⁻¹ is Jₑ⁻¹, not A⁻¹. Assume the required blocks are invertible.

Interpret the subtraction

Some parameter effects can imitate each other.

If moving the target changes all ranges similarly, an unknown offset can explain part of that same change.

The Schur complement removes information that cannot distinguish position from the nuisance parameter.

No loss when the coupling b is zero. A large loss is possible for clustered lines of sight.
notes: For z_i=||p−a_i||+β+ε_i with common σ, A=Σuᵢuᵢᵀ/σ², b=Σuᵢ/σ², and c=m/σ². Thus J_e=(Σuᵢuᵢᵀ−(Σuᵢ)(Σuᵢ)ᵀ/m)/σ². This is exactly the toggle implemented in the geometry lab. The clock-offset analogy uses β in distance units, so a time offset would be multiplied by propagation speed first. The block A is conditional information when β is known; inverting only A when β is unknown is overly optimistic. Orthogonal parameter coupling can make the loss zero.

title: A moving support breaks the familiar proof.
subtitle: Not every model allows differentiation to pass through the expectation.
body:
A useful warning example

Xi ∼ Uniform(0, θ)

The boundary moves with θ. The omitted boundary contribution is exactly why the score argument fails.

Do not force the shortcut

Check the estimator directly.

This variance is obtained from the sample maximum’s distribution—not from the invalid regular CRB calculation.

Other warning signs: boundaries, nondifferentiability, singular information, and misspecified noise.
notes: Here X_(n) is the sample maximum. Its expectation is nθ/(n+1) and its variance is nθ²/((n+1)²(n+2)); multiplying by (n+1)/n gives the displayed unbiased estimator and variance. For example n=4 gives variance θ²/24. Blindly using E[U²]=n²/θ² and then applying the regular unbiased inequality would suggest θ²/n², which is contradicted by this unbiased estimator precisely because E[U]≠0 and the regular score identity fails. Parameter-independent support is a common sufficient regularity condition, not a necessary condition for every possible information inequality. A nonregular model needs a suitable alternative argument.

title: Design the experiment, not only the estimator.
subtitle: A new independent, correctly modeled measurement adds a positive-semidefinite information term.
body:
Linear Gaussian measurements

H controls sensitivity and geometry.
R controls noise and correlation.

Both matter. Counting measurements alone is not enough.

Choose a design objective

Different questions favor different designs.

Design goalOne common criterion
Small total varianceMinimize tr(J⁻¹)
Small ellipsoid volumeMaximize log det J
Protect the weakest directionMaximize λmin(J)

Use a well-defined parameterization and units. These are local design criteria at the assumed true state.
notes: The displayed linear Gaussian formula assumes R is known, positive definite, and independent of θ. With parameter-dependent covariance the general Gaussian information also contains covariance-derivative terms. For full column-rank H, generalized least squares is unbiased and attains this CRB exactly. For nonlinear h(θ), replace H by the Jacobian evaluated at θ to compute the local information for this additive Gaussian model; this does not guarantee that a nonlinear estimator attains the bound. Trace, determinant, and minimum-eigenvalue criteria describe different uncertainty summaries and can depend strongly on scaling the parameter coordinates. The objective choices are derived from the covariance ellipsoid.

title: Read a CRB result like a careful reviewer.
subtitle: Before comparing an algorithm with a bound, make sure they solve the same statistical problem.
body:
01 · Estimator class

Is the comparison valid?

Measure or analyze bias. A learned, constrained, or regularized estimator is not automatically unbiased.

02 · Parameter vector

What was treated as known?

Include unknown offsets, calibration, orientation, or other nuisance parameters before inverting.

03 · Metric and model

Are the units and assumptions aligned?

Match variance with variance, MSE with MSE, and RMSE with a square-root bound. Model correlations correctly.

04 · Local versus global

What can the bound miss?

Inspect rank, conditioning, competing solutions, and low-information regimes. A small local CRB is not a guarantee of successful localization.
notes: Four common mistakes are comparing the unbiased CRB against a biased estimator’s MSE without qualification; omitting nuisance variables; plotting an RMSE against a variance lower bound; and interpreting a well-conditioned local Hessian as proof of global identifiability. A finite Monte Carlo estimate is also random: use enough trials and report uncertainty. The demo intentionally makes these caveats visible rather than hiding them behind attractive ellipses. The CRB is a diagnostic and design tool, not an algorithm or a universal confidence interval.

title: Three ideas to keep.
subtitle: More information lowers the bound. Bias changes the comparison. Geometry decides the weak directions.
body:
01 · Sensitivity

Information belongs to the experiment.

The same estimator can face very different limits under different noise or measurement designs.

02 · Precision

Unbiased variance has a floor.

A better algorithm cannot beat this floor while remaining in the theorem’s estimator class.

03 · Direction

The matrix tells you where.

Independent, complementary measurements are often more valuable than repeated views of the same direction.
notes: Return to the opening question. There are two distinct levers: choose a better estimator for the available data, or improve what the data reveal through sensing design. A CRB gap does not automatically show algorithmic weakness: finite-sample nonattainability, bias, nuisance variables, or model mismatch may explain it. Close with the demonstration that moving anchors changes the information before running any localization algorithm. Optional discussion: which nuisance parameter or correlation is easiest to overlook in the audience’s own application?

notes: Source mapping: S1 grounds the scalar proof, Gaussian calculation, and efficiency discussion. S2 gives broad information and estimation context. S3 grounds localization-information geometry and equivalent Fisher information; this deck’s independent Gaussian-range toy model is deliberately simpler than that paper’s waveform-level model. S4 supports the carefully qualified asymptotic MLE statement. The biased extension, uniform-maximum calculation, linear Gaussian design consequences, figures, and numerical demos are independently derived teaching examples. Links navigate in the same tab, following the site convention. The existing site’s warm paper, Georgia headings, and restrained teal/blue/rust palette informed the visual design.
